title: Nepal Flood Death Toll Hits 538 as Barrier Lake Threatens Fresh Devastation
excerpt: Nearly 1,000 remain missing including 98 Indians, while Kathmandu declines foreign search-and-rescue teams and a debris-dammed lake on the Tibet border begins to overflow.
body:
• Nepal's death toll from Wednesday's glacier collapse floods has reached 538, with 977 people still missing including 622 foreign nationals
  • A barrier lake formed by debris on the Tibet side has begun overflowing, forcing temporary halts to rescue operations and fresh evacuation alerts
  • Nepal has declined offers of search-and-rescue teams from India, the US, China and five other nations, saying its own security forces are handling operations

The death toll from Nepal's catastrophic flash floods has climbed to 538, with 977 people still missing, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said on Friday. The disaster, triggered by a massive glacier collapse on the Nepal-China border on Wednesday, has affected more than 90,000 people across multiple districts.

Among the missing are 622 foreign nationals, including 98 Indians and 65 Americans, according to Nepal's Tourism Board. A total of 117 tourists have been rescued so far, including 85 Indian nationals. Some 14,829 security personnel are deployed across the worst-hit areas, and 3,742 people have been pulled to safety.

Barrier Lake Raises Risk of Second Flood Wave

Rescue operations have been repeatedly disrupted by the threat of fresh flooding from a barrier lake that formed on the Tibet side of the border after Wednesday's disaster. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported Friday that the dammed lake — holding an estimated 2.5 million cubic meters of water — had begun overflowing.

Nepal police issued a fresh alert after receiving reports that a dam on the Tibet side had burst. Authorities halted helicopter rescue operations and ordered personnel and civilians to move to higher ground.

"We can see that the level of water in the river is rising."

— Narendra Pariyar, Chief District Officer, Rasuwa

Operations resumed after authorities assessed the immediate threat as manageable, but rescue teams remain on high alert for another surge of water, mud and debris.

Kathmandu Declines Foreign Rescue Offers

In a move that drew international attention, Nepal's Foreign Ministry on Friday declined offers of search-and-rescue teams from India, China, the United States, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

"The offer for help is natural. Our security agencies are doing the search-and-rescue operation. For now we don't require such help."

— Lok Bahadur Chhetri, Nepal Foreign Ministry Spokesperson

South Korea, which has nine nationals missing and 10 stranded at a flood-hit hydropower plant, pushed back on the decision. Seoul pledged $1 million in humanitarian assistance and said it would "keep negotiating with Nepal over the matter."

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ambassador to the United Nations, told Reuters the reluctance may be linked to the proximity of Rasuwa district to China's Tibet — one of Beijing's most sensitive territorial issues. Nepal's Foreign Ministry denied any Chinese influence on the decision.

India Sends Relief as 98 Nationals Remain Missing

India has dispatched nearly 50 metric tons of disaster-relief supplies in two tranches, including temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, lamps and medicines, according to India's Ministry of External Affairs. New Delhi also offered to send search-and-rescue teams, which Nepal declined.

The disaster struck a region popular with Hindu pilgrims traveling to sacred Mount Kailash in Tibet. Many of the missing Indians were in transit along the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor when the flood hit on Wednesday.

Scientists Point to Glacier Collapse

Experts believe a vast quantity of rock and ice fell from around 16,000 feet — possibly due to the partial collapse of a glacier — and plunged 4,000 feet into the valley below. The impact turned ice into a devastating wave of water that barreled through river valleys in Nepal and Tibet, carrying debris as far as 150 miles downstream to districts near Nepal's southern border with India.

The flood levelled entire towns, destroyed bridges, damaged hydropower plants and severed road access across the Rasuwa, Sindhupalchok, Dhading and Nuwakot districts. Army personnel were also working to rescue workers trapped inside a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa, where thick mud complicated efforts.

Global Response Mobilizes

Beyond India, the international community has stepped in with financial aid. The UK pledged £5 million ($6.79 million) along with emergency responders. The United States is sending a disaster response adviser and $500,000 in funds. The Red Cross released 1 million Swiss francs ($1.24 million) in emergency funding, and the WHO dispatched medical supplies.

China's Premier Li Qiang visited the disaster site at Gyirong on Thursday. On the Chinese side of the border, five deaths have been confirmed with 558 people still missing, according to state news agency Xinhua.
nri_angle: 98 Indian nationals remain missing and 85 have been rescued; India sent 50 metric tons of relief supplies but Nepal declined its offer of search-and-rescue teams.
author: Diaspora Desk
